title: Canarsie Traditional Land
summary: Canarsie carries the name of a Native community whose homeland included parts of present-day Brooklyn and Jamaica Bay. Generations lived from and cared for these shores before Dutch and English settlement brought dispossession. Lenape people continue in their homeland and beyond it, including through Native-led cultural work in New York. The name is a reminder of that enduring relationship: its people did not disappear as the city grew.
why_this_matters: Canarsie Traditional Land presents Brooklyn and western Long Island as Native homeland. The page connects place names, colonial records, Lenape-related language context, and public memory without reducing Canarsie history to a myth of disappearance.
introduction_title: Canarsie ancestry beneath and within the city
introduction_content:
Canarsie, also recorded as Canarsee, connects the modern neighborhood to the older Native geography of Brooklyn and Jamaica Bay. Colonial grants, petitions and patents in the history below record a struggle over inhabited land. Reading them only as a sequence of property transfers obscures the communities whose land became the city.

Today, Lenape people speak for their own history through institutions such as Lenape Center. Its Native founders and cultural leaders connect present-day nations with work in New York through art, education, language and public history. That continuance is shared; the surviving records are not detailed enough to trace every Canarsie family. An acknowledgment can be honest about the limits of the surviving records while recognizing that displacement and changed community names do not amount to disappearance.

Sources for ancestry and continuance: National Park Service; Lenape Center. See References for citations and the historical sources used below.
history_title: Canarsie In Dutch And English Records
history_content: Seventeenth-century Dutch and English records preserve Canarsie-related names in grants, petitions, and patent descriptions. These records show Native land relationships being translated into colonial property systems while Canarsie people remained part of western Long Island political and cultural history. Later histories sometimes turned Canarsie into folklore or disappearance stories.
